---
title: "Health is not stationary"
---

*This page frames an assumption that runs through the whole project: the
state of health, and everything associated with it, changes over time.
It is reflected in every milestone of the [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md).*

## What nonstationarity means here

A quantity is **stationary** if its statistical properties — average
level, variability, relationships with other variables — stay the same
over time; **nonstationary** means they drift: the average moves, the
variability changes, or the relationships themselves change
[@box2015; @hyndman2021].

The project assumes BC's health is nonstationary in all three senses:

1. **The outcome drifts.** Life expectancy, disease burden, mental
   health, and functional status trend, oscillate, and jump. Secular
   improvements, epidemics (including the COVID-19 pandemic [@whocovid]
   and the toxic drug crisis in BC [@bccdcDrugs]), demographic aging,
   and policy or health-system reforms all move the level — sometimes
   gradually, sometimes as abrupt regime shifts.
2. **Relationships drift.** A variable associated with health in one
   decade need not be associated in the next. Income gradients, the
   effect of health-system capacity, and behavioural risk factors all
   operate in a changing context; a pooled estimate over many years may
   describe no actual period well.
3. **The data-generating process drifts.** Even when health itself is
   unchanged, the *measurement* changes: coding definitions, survey
   methods, coverage, and reporting practice evolve. Part of any apparent
   change in a series is change in how it was recorded.

## What this rules out

The intuitive way to report "the state of health" is a snapshot: this is
BC's number, here is how it compares. A dynamic view rejects the
snapshot as the headline:

- **Levels without trajectories hide the direction.** A stable-looking
  level can be the crossing point of rising and falling trends in
  subpopulations.
- **Single pooled estimates hide instability.** A decade-long average
  association can be the blend of two periods with different — even
  opposite — relationships.
- **Undated conclusions rot.** A finding true for 2000–2019 may be false
  for 2020 onward, but reads identically unless its window is stated.

## What follows for each stage of the project

- **Definition (M1).** Health is defined as a time-varying state with
  temporal semantics — a trajectory with levels, slopes, and possible
  discontinuities — not a timeless attribute.
- **Data (M2).** Catalogues record coverage windows, refresh cadence,
  revisions, and definitional breaks; series are checked for structural
  breaks before use.
- **Description (M3).** Trends, turning points, and change points are
  reported alongside levels; regimes (pre- and post-shock) are compared
  explicitly rather than blended.
- **Dependence (M4).** Associations are estimated over stated windows
  and tested for stability before any pooled number is reported.
- **Causation (M5).** Causal structures are time-indexed: lagged
  effects, feedback loops, and time-varying confounding are represented,
  and each causal claim carries a validity window.
- **Recommendations (M6).** Every recommendation is dated, tied to the
  window of evidence behind it, and paired with the drift indicators
  that would trigger re-evaluation.

## The practical consequence: re-run, don't just publish once

If health is nonstationary, publishing an analysis is not the end of the
job. The pipeline must be re-runnable as new data arrive, and results
versioned with their observation window — so that "what is the state of
health in BC?" can be answered again, differently, when it *has* changed.
This is a cross-cutting concern in the roadmap: vigilance about
drift applies to every milestone, not once at the end.
